newsitem.title: IRAN: Storm clouds gather over Khatami's cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Storm clouds gather over Khatami's cabinet.

text.p: Storm clouds are starting to gather over some of Iranian President Mohammad Khatami's choices for cabinet positions.

Khatami's opponents in the conservative-led Majlis or parliament were reported in Iranian newspapers on Wednesday as saying they would be reluctant to pass a necessary vote of confidence on a core of potentially reformist ministers.

The 54-year-old moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric, elected into office on a mandate of introducing social and economic freedoms, on Tuesday presented his list of 22 cabinet nominees to the 270-seat parliament.
Parliament will begin debating the merits of each of the nominees and their legislative programmes on August 19.

But some conservative parliament members are already indicating that Khatami could be in for a disappointment on a number of key portfolios including the sensitive positions of culture, interior and even foreign affairs ministers.

"I don't think that Mr. Khatami is going to be able to perform the miracles the people expect of him. I'm rather worried about the next four years," rightist deputy Ahmad Rasoolnejad told the Iran News daily paper.

Khatami's landslide election victory in May was mainly secured by the support of Iranian youth, women and the middle- class on expectations that the moderate cleric would ease daily restrictions in life, such as stern dress codes.
His nomination of Ataollah Mohajerani as minister of culture and Islamic guidance provoked strong opposition in some conservative Iranian papers.
"He (Mohajerani) is very unlikely to be approved by the Majlis and he will most probably be replaced," an unnamed parliament member told the Tehran Times.

The 43-year-old Mohajerani, trained as a historian, has faced increasingly sharp criticism from conservatives after he advocated direct talks with the United States in 1990 and pressed for more cultural freedoms.
The culture ministry plays a key role in domestic life in Iran since it has power over the type of books that can be printed and the extent of media freedom.
If Khatami fails to secure his own appointee at culture, high expectations among the electorate of new freedoms in the 18-year-old Islamic republic could be dashed, analysts said.

"The weak point of the cabinet is that some members do not have a strong ideological basis and their backgrounds show tolerance to the world arrogance (the West)," the conservative Abrar newspaper said in an editorial.
Abrar quoted conservative parliament member Nafiseh Fayazbakhsh as saying that problems could arise over who would fill the posts of culture, interior, oil and also education.
Iran News also reported that conservatives in parliament had warned they would block the nomination of both Mohajerani and interior ministry nominee Abdollah Nouri.
Local conservative papers have said that Khatami's candidate for foreign affairs -- United Nations ambassador Kamal Kharrazi -- could also spark rejection from parliament members.

"It is not fitting that a person who has lived in the United States, whether as a student or as U.N. ambassador, to be in charge of the foreign policy of a nation that considers the United States its greatest enemy," the hardline Jomhuri Eslami said prior to Khatami's cabinet submission on Tuesday.
Moderate, pro-Khatami parliament members said they expected the Majlis to accept the president's nominations because the list included people from across the political spectrum.
